newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Sales slump seen clinching Australia rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Sales slump seen clinching Australia rate cut.

text.p: Odds on a cut in Australian interest rates shortened further Friday when data on retail sales showed shoppers shunned the malls in September.

Retail turnover plunged 3.7 percent to A$10.05 billion when the market had been betting on a modest 0.5 percent dip. This was the biggest monthly drop since April 1994 and promised to sharply reduce the contribution sales were expected to make to economic growth in the September quarter.
"I think a rate cut next week looks highly probable," said Stephen Koukoulas, senior economist at Citibank Australia.

The Reserve Bank of Australia holds its monthly board meeting on Tuesday to discuss policy and speculation has been rampant for weeks that it would sanction a 0.5 point cut in official cash rates to 6.5 percent.
The sales figures were only the latest in a run of weak data recently which has caused analysts to seriously review their assumptions about the economy's health.

"When you combine this with the skilled vacancy survey, poor exports in the balance of payments data, the building approvals numbers, and the CPI numbers it is all pointing now to a very weak economy," said Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson.
"I think the chance of a rate cut next week is now better than a 50-50 chance," said Henderson. "I can't see a lot can be gained now by holding off for another month."
Some even thought the omens were gloomy enough to suggest an easing of more than 0.5 point was needed, perhaps in one go or more likely in two stages of half point.
"Combined with low inflation and signs that wages growth is slowing, this definitely points to the Reserve Bank easing," said Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP Investments.
"I think there'll now be a bit more debate about the magnitude of that easing," he added.
The money market was already contemplating such a scenario and pushed the March 90-day bank bill future contract to 93.70, implying they saw scope for rates to hit 6.30 percent or lower.

The only caveat analysts offered was the RBA's expressed concern over the high level of some enterprise wage agreements, a worry the bank explicitly highlighted in its September quarter economic bulletin just a fortnight ago.

"It might be hard for the bank to cut credibly without some sign enterprise bargains are slowing," said Andrew Ticehurst, an economist at Macquarie Bank. "So they may wait to see the latest figures on wages in late November and tie a cut to that."
Whatever the timing, the need for an easing in policy was rarely doubted, especially now once free-spending Australian consumers seemed to be tightening their purse strings.

The steep fall in sales in September more than wiped out gains of 1.1 and 1.0 percent in August and July respectively and saw annual retail growth slow to just 2.0 percent from 5.0 percent the month before.

Some analysts cautioned the sheer size of the fall looked suspicious, although the Bureau of Statistics said they had no reason to doubt the validity of the survey. The Bureau did think that the early timing of Father's Day biased the result.
Since Father's Day fell on September 1 it meant all the spending on ties and socks and the like came in August instead of September, thus boosting one at the expense of the other.

Sales for the September quarter were still up 0.6 percent when adjusted for inflation, but that was only half the 1.3 percent expected. That meant sales would make only about 0.1 point contribution to the expenditure based measure of Gross Domestic Product when analysts had looked for 0.3 to 0.4 point.
"It means we are not going to get as much contribution from retail trade as we thought, so we are looking at a weaker growth story," summed up Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust.
